title: Age-Appropriate Chores: A By-Age Guide (2 to Teen)
meta_description: Which chores fit each age, from toddler to teen, explained by a dad of four and foster parent. Pick your child's age for a free chart built just for them.
intro: The phrase "age-appropriate chores" gets searched a lot, and I think it's because most of us sense the truth behind it: a job that fits a four-year-old is wasted on a fourteen-year-old, and a teen's responsibilities would crush a preschooler. So there's no one master list to print out — there's a ladder, and your kid stands on a different rung every couple of years. I'm Andrew. My wife and I are raising four (right now they run from a nine-year-old boy up to an eighteen-year-old), and during one stretch we also fostered three little ones as toddlers, so we've climbed this ladder from the very bottom more than once. Use the age picker just below to land on a chart sized for your child, with every per-age chart linked out so you can compare. Before you do, let me hand you the thinking that makes those charts actually work — what shifts from one stage to the next, how to choose a rung your kid can stand on, and why, in our home, none of it runs on bribes.

sections.heading: Why the right chores change as kids grow up
sections.body:
It helps to stop picturing chores as tasks and start picturing them as rehearsals for being a grown-up. Once I made that switch in my own head, the by-age progression stopped feeling arbitrary. You're not trying to get the dishwasher emptied; you're trying, over fifteen or so years, to graduate a capable adult. Every rung is just the next rehearsal that child is ready for.

With our littlest ones, roughly two through four, the rehearsal is about their own body and their own stuff — wrestling into clothes, managing a toothbrush, scooping the blocks back into the bin. The smart play here is to invite rather than require. When a toddler grabs at whatever you're using because copying you is the whole point of being two, let them, and teach a single motion. Nobody walks away with a clean room. You walk away with a kid who, a year or two on, treats helping as ordinary.

From about five to seven, a chore stops being play and becomes a small obligation. We hand over a shared-space job or two here and brace ourselves to redo it, because the finished product is beside the point. What lands at this age is the idea that the home is a shared thing and everyone in it has a part to keep it going.

Through the middle stretch, eight to twelve, capability finally catches the expectation. Real dishes, real trash duty, lending a hand with dinner, and outdoor work for the ones who lean that way. Our son tags along on every fix-it project I take on, firing off question after question, and you can practically watch the skill stack up. The work gets bigger because the child finally can.

Then come the teens, and I'll be honest with you: the chart that hummed along at nine quietly collapses around thirteen. We've shepherded two kids through that already with two more closing in. The whole arrangement has to mature into something closer to grown-up accountability — agreed-upon contributions, real freedom, and a lot less hovering from us. The teen page lays out exactly how we rebuilt it once the old chart gave out.

sections.heading: Picking a rung your child can actually stand on
sections.body:
Their age points you to a starting rung, and for a lot of families that pick is exactly right. But the number on a birthday cake is a suggestion, not a verdict — so look at the actual kid before you commit.

If chores are brand-new in your house, or you've already watched a chart die a slow death on the fridge door, set the bar a notch under their age instead of right at it. A child who's never been held to a routine grows into a slightly easier list and feels the win; hand that same child a list pitched to their exact age and you're often setting up a quiet failure you'll both resent. Bumping things up later is a celebration. Walking a discouraged kid back down is a much harder day.

Here's the other piece almost no list mentions: a system only earns its keep if it survives a normal, messy life. We used to build something tidy and watch the first holiday week or stomach bug knock it flat — and the temptation was always to call the whole thing a failure. It wasn't failing; it just wasn't built to take a hit and recover. So pick a rung that's easy to climb back onto after the week falls apart, not the most impressive one you can imagine on a calm Sunday. Choose the age, run it for a week or two, and nudge it higher the moment it starts feeling routine.

sections.heading: The chart works for you, not against the kid
sections.body:
Every per-age chart on this site rests on one conviction, and I'd rather say it out loud than let you guess. The chart is a parent's instrument — a way to keep an honest read on how each child is doing and to notice when it's time to lean in. It was never meant to dangle a prize in front of a kid to buy a few minutes of cooperation.

That framing changes what you do when the wheels wobble. The reflex is to up the ante — a bigger reward, a screen-time deal. We pull the opposite lever and lean back on the plain expectation: in this family, everybody pitches in, and that one isn't on the negotiating table. Treats, downtime, and screens stay walled off from the chore list on purpose. We don't make our kids earn their fun by laboring for it, and we don't ring up jobs one at a time like groceries.

There is an allowance in our house, but it's not a payout per job. It rides on the whole picture — whether the work is done carefully, done dependably, and done without a sour attitude across a stretch of weeks. The instant a chore becomes a sale, a kid learns to haggle over the price. When pitching in is simply what it means to belong here, that haggling never starts, and the chart gets to be what it was always for: your clear-eyed view of how the family's doing.

faq.q: What are age-appropriate chores at each age?
faq.a: In broad strokes: ages two to four are about self-care, like getting dressed, brushing teeth, and clearing their own mess. Ages five to seven take on light shared-space jobs such as wiping a counter or setting the table, and you'll often quietly redo the work. Ages eight to twelve handle dishes, trash, cooking help, and outdoor work as their skills grow. Teens move to bigger, more independent responsibilities. Pick your child's exact age in the picker above to see the specific list built for that stage rather than guessing at it.

faq.q: How do I know if a chore is too advanced for my child's age?
faq.a: Watch what happens when you assign it. If the task ends in tears, constant reminders, or a job you fully take over every time, it's likely a rung too high for now — drop down a level so your child can finish it on their own and feel the win, then raise it once it's easy. We learned this most sharply as foster parents: the toddlers we cared for settled fastest when the daily steps were simple, predictable, and repeated the same way every day. A level a child can hit reliably beats an ambitious one they can't.

faq.q: Should I assign chores by age or by ability?
faq.a: Use age to set a sensible starting point, then adjust to the real child in front of you. The age picker gives you a developmentally reasonable baseline. If your child is new to chores, or a past chart fizzled out, begin one rung lower so success comes consistently, then climb as the work gets routine. We've found the strongest systems are the ones that bounce back after a busy week or a holiday knocks them sideways — so favor a level your child can restart easily over one that only looks good on paper.
